claims.text: In-situ substrate pre-heating during laser powder bed fusion of AlCrFeNiSi reduces residual thermal stresses relative to builds without pre-heating.
In-situ substrate pre-heating refines the microstructure of laser-powder-bed-fused AlCrFeNiSi.
The microstructural refinement caused by substrate pre-heating improves mechanical properties.
Standard additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi without substrate pre-heating typically produces high thermal gradients.
Standard additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi without substrate pre-heating typically produces residual stresses.
Standard additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi without substrate pre-heating typically results in degraded mechanical properties.
The proposed processing window is a build-platform temperature of 300–400 °C, a scanning speed of about 1000 mm/s, and a layer thickness of 20–30 μm.
An inert or controlled atmosphere mitigates oxidation risks during elevated-temperature substrate pre-heating.
Substrate pre-heating reduces thermal gradients and stabilizes melt-pool solidification.
Reduced thermal gradients and stabilized melt-pool solidification produce a more uniform phase transformation.
Reducing the temperature differential between the melt pool and substrate reduces thermal shock during solidification.
Reduced thermal shock produces slower contraction rates.
Slower contraction produces a refined microstructure with lower dislocation density.
A refined microstructure with lower dislocation density lessens residual stress and prevents mechanical-property degradation.
Pre-heated components will have significantly lower residual stress than components produced with ambient-temperature substrates.
Pre-heated components will exhibit improved yield strength relative to conventionally produced components.
Pre-heated components will exhibit improved ductility relative to conventionally produced components.
Substrate pre-heating will eliminate the need for post-process stress-relief steps.
The hypothesis applies to miniature AlCrFeNiSi components produced by laser powder bed fusion within a substrate-temperature window of 300–400 °C.
Oxidation or unintended phase transformations at elevated substrate temperatures could offset the predicted improvements.
